paper.title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection

read_sources.note: Used for metadata, authors, abstract, revision history, and headline taxonomy/results.
Read for threat model, injection methods, tool/API attack surface, synthetic and Bing Chat evaluations, limitations, and mitigation discussion.
Used to confirm demonstration categories, repository purpose, and released attack scenarios.

summary.one_sentence: Indirect prompt injection lets an attacker hide instructions in content that an LLM application later retrieves, causing the model to treat untrusted data as control input.
summary.thesis: The paper's security insight is that retrieval and tool use collapse the data/instruction boundary: when an LLM reads hostile webpages, emails, code comments, or documents, those inputs can steer the application and its APIs.
summary.why_it_matters: For agents, this is the confused-deputy problem in natural language. The model acts with the user's authority while consuming text controlled by other parties.

prior_state: Early prompt-injection discussions mostly assumed the attacker directly prompts their own model session.
LLM-integrated applications increasingly retrieve webpages, documents, emails, code, and search results at inference time.
Agents and application-integrated LLMs can call tools or APIs on behalf of a user.
Existing input/output filters do not cleanly distinguish untrusted retrieved data from trusted instructions.
problem.key_gap: The paper asks what happens when the attacker is not the user, but controls data that the user's LLM application will later retrieve and process.
assumptions: Retrieved data can contain natural-language instructions that the model may follow.
The model's instruction-following capability can be redirected by content from untrusted sources.
Tool/API access increases impact because model behavior can cause external side effects.
Current mitigations are incomplete and often brittle against obfuscation or encoded instructions.

concepts.name: Indirect prompt injection
concepts.definition: An attack where malicious instructions are placed in external data that a victim's LLM application later retrieves and ingests.

concepts.name: LLM-integrated application
concepts.definition: An application that embeds an LLM and connects it to retrieval, tools, APIs, memory, or other user-facing functions.

concepts.name: Data/instruction boundary
concepts.definition: The intended separation between untrusted content to be summarized or used as data and trusted instructions that govern application behavior.

concepts.name: Retrieved prompt
concepts.definition: Prompt-like text embedded in retrieved content such as a webpage, email, source file, or document.

concepts.name: Tool confused deputy
concepts.definition: A situation where the LLM uses a user's tool authority to carry out instructions supplied by an untrusted third party.

concepts.name: Prompt worming
concepts.definition: A scenario where an injected instruction causes the application to spread the prompt to other systems or future sessions.

method.core_idea: Model LLM applications as systems that retrieve untrusted text and call tools, classify indirect injection delivery and impacts, then demonstrate attacks against controlled synthetic applications and real-world systems.
action_grammar: attacker content: webpage, email, code comment, file, or other data containing hidden or visible instructions.
retrieval event: user query or application workflow pulls attacker content into the model context.
model ingestion: the LLM processes retrieved text as part of the same context as trusted instructions.
tool/API action: the LLM decides whether and how to call search, email, memory, URL retrieval, code completion, or other interfaces.
impact: data theft, manipulation, persistence, denial of service, social engineering, worming, or misinformation.
mitigation: filtering, supervision, less capable rescuer models, moderation, interpretability, or architectural restriction.
steps: Define indirect prompt injection as malicious prompt delivery through retrieved external data.
Map injection methods: passive retrieval, active delivery such as email, user-driven copy/paste, hidden content, encoded payloads, and multi-stage retrieval.
Map threat classes including data theft, remote control, persistence, worming, fraud, disinformation, and availability attacks.
Build synthetic LLM applications with tools such as search, view, URL retrieval, email, address book, and memory.
Test attacks on synthetic applications and black-box real-world systems such as Bing Chat and code-completion contexts.
Discuss limitations, disclosure, and mitigations while noting that robust defenses remain unresolved.
method.pseudocode:
attacker.publish(content_with_hidden_instruction)

user.ask(agent, task)
retrieved = search_or_tool_fetch(task)
context = trusted_system_prompt + user_task + retrieved

action = llm(context)
if action.calls_tool:
    tool.execute(action, user_authority)

# The attacker did not prompt the model directly; retrieved data crossed the control boundary.

claims.statement: LLM-integrated applications blur the line between data and instructions when they retrieve untrusted content into the model context.
caveats: The degree of vulnerability depends on model behavior, prompt design, tool authority, and retrieval path.

claims.statement: Indirect prompt injection enables remote attackers without direct model access to influence a victim's LLM application by poisoning likely retrieved data.
caveats: Successful delivery requires the poisoned content to be retrieved and accepted into context.

claims.statement: The attack surface includes passive retrieval, active delivery through channels like email, user-driven delivery, hidden prompts, encoded prompts, and multi-stage payloads.
caveats: Some methods were demonstrated qualitatively rather than with large-scale success-rate measurement.

claims.statement: Indirect prompt injection can enable remote control, data theft, persistence, worming, social engineering, misinformation, and availability attacks in LLM-integrated systems.
caveats: Impact severity depends heavily on connected tools and privileges.

claims.statement: The paper demonstrates attacks in synthetic GPT-3/GPT-4-style applications and against real-world systems including Bing Chat and code-completion contexts.
caveats: Real-world evaluations were necessarily limited and often qualitative due to black-box systems and ethical constraints.

claims.statement: When the LLM controls tool/API calls, retrieved prompts can manipulate not only generated text but also the timing, content, and direction of external API use.
caveats: Applications with no external tools have lower side-effect risk, but still face misinformation or persuasion risks.

claims.statement: The paper argues that effective mitigations were lacking and that RLHF, filtering, LLM supervisors, and retrieved-input scanning are brittle or unresolved defenses.
caveats: The mitigation landscape has evolved since 2023, but the architectural boundary problem remains central.

evidence.result: The authors argue that retrieval-augmented LLM applications blur data and instruction boundaries, making untrusted external text capable of steering model behavior.
Adversaries can place prompts in data likely to be retrieved, remotely affecting a victim's application without directly prompting it.
The paper describes passive retrieval, active email-like delivery, user-driven injection, hidden prompt content, multi-stage payloads, and Base64/encoded injections.

The paper and repository describe impacts including remote control, leaking user data, persistent compromise, spreading injections, social engineering, code-completion attacks, and availability disruption.
The authors build synthetic applications with search, view, URL retrieval, email, address book, and memory tools, and test attacks against Bing Chat and code-completion contexts.
The authors show that processing retrieved prompts can manipulate application functionality and control whether and how APIs are called.

The paper discusses RLHF, input/output filtering, retrieved-input filtering, LLM supervisors, and interpretability-style outlier detection, concluding that robust defenses and their resilience to obfuscation require more work.

agent_infra_takeaways: Treat retrieved content as hostile data, never as authority-bearing instructions.
A model should not be the only boundary between untrusted text and privileged tools.
Tool calls need capability scoping, confirmation, policy checks, audit logs, and least privilege independent of prompt intent.
Memory can make prompt injection persistent; stored notes and retrieved history need the same distrust as webpages or emails.
Defenses should be architectural: data provenance, content labeling, separate planning/execution authority, sandboxed tools, and explicit user approval for side effects.
Prompt injection is closer to confused-deputy and capability-security failure than to ordinary bad prompting.
caveats: Many demonstrations are qualitative proof-of-concepts rather than statistically measured benchmark results.
The real-world systems tested were black boxes and have changed since 2023.
The paper intentionally avoided seeding public sources with live malicious prompts for ethical reasons.
Some mitigations and product defenses have improved since publication, but no general clean fix is established by the paper.
The attack requires delivery: hostile content must be retrieved, included in context, and granted enough influence to affect output or tools.
Impact depends on connected privileges; read-only summarizers differ from agents that can send email, write memory, or call APIs.
